section.title: Water into Wine and the Temple
section.sectionRationale: John pairs two opening scenes that announce the new order Jesus brings. At Cana He turns water for ritual washing into the best wine, the first of His signs, revealing His glory. In Jerusalem He cleanses the temple and points to the true temple, His own body, to be destroyed and raised in three days. Old vessels and old temple give way to the joy and presence Jesus Himself embodies.
section.thesis: In His first sign Jesus transforms the water of ritual purification into the abundant wine of the messianic feast, revealing His glory, and in cleansing the temple He announces that the true meeting place with God is His own body, to be destroyed and raised, so that both scenes proclaim a new order centered on Him.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the wedding at Cana where water becomes wine and glory is revealed; the cleansing of the temple and the demand for a sign; and the riddle of the temple of His body, with a closing note that Jesus knew what was in every heart.

units.label: The wedding at Cana
units.note: the first sign, His glory revealed

verses.text: On the third day a wedding took place at Cana in Galilee. Jesus’ mother was there,
and Jesus and His disciples had also been invited to the wedding.
When the wine ran out, Jesus’ mother said to Him, “They have no more wine.”
“Woman, what is that to you and to Me?” Jesus replied. “My {{hora|hour}} has not yet come.”
His mother said to the servants, “Do whatever He tells you.”
Now six stone water jars had been set there for the Jewish rites of purification. Each could hold from twenty to thirty gallons.
Jesus told the servants, “Fill the jars with water.” So they filled them to the brim.
“Now draw some out,” He said, “and take it to the master of the banquet.” They did so,
and the master of the banquet tasted the water that had been turned into wine. He did not know where it was from, but the servants who had drawn the water knew. Then he called the bridegroom aside
and said, “Everyone serves the fine wine first, and then the cheap wine after the guests are drunk. But you have saved the fine wine until now!”
Jesus performed this, the first of His {{semeion|signs}}, at Cana in Galilee. He thus revealed His {{doxa|glory}}, and His disciples believed in Him.

units.label: Cleansing the temple
units.note: My Father's house is not a marketplace

verses.text: After this, He went down to Capernaum with His mother and brothers and His disciples, and they stayed there a few days.
When the Jewish Passover was near, Jesus went up to Jerusalem.
In the temple courts He found men selling cattle, sheep, and doves, and money changers seated at their tables.
So He made a whip out of cords and drove all from the temple courts, both sheep and cattle. He poured out the coins of the money changers and overturned their tables.
To those selling doves He said, “Get these out of here! How dare you turn My Father’s house into a marketplace!”
His disciples remembered that it is written: “Zeal for Your house will consume Me.”

units.label: The temple of His body
units.note: destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up

verses.text: On account of this, the Jews demanded, “What sign can You show us to prove Your authority to do these things?”
Jesus answered, “Destroy this {{naos|temple}}, and in three days I will raise it up again.”
“This temple took forty-six years to build,” the Jews replied, “and You are going to raise it up in three days?”
But Jesus was speaking about the temple of His body.
After He was raised from the dead, His disciples remembered that He had said this. Then they believed the Scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken.
While He was in Jerusalem at the Passover Feast, many people saw the signs He was doing and believed in His name.
But Jesus did not entrust Himself to them, for He knew them all.
He did not need any testimony about man, for He knew what was in a man.

hora.gloss: Hour, appointed time. In John the hour is a technical term for the appointed moment of Jesus' death and glorification. At Cana He says His hour has not yet come; through the Gospel the hour approaches, until in the upper room He declares that the hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified. Everything moves toward that hour at the cross.

semeion.gloss: Sign. John does not call Jesus' miracles wonders but signs, because each one points beyond itself to who Jesus is and to the life He gives. The Gospel is structured around seven such signs, beginning here at Cana. A sign is meant to be read, so that seeing the act leads to believing in the person and receiving life.

doxa.gloss: Glory, the visible weight and splendor of God's presence. The prologue said the disciples beheld His glory; the first sign is where that glory begins to be revealed in action, and His disciples believed. In John this glory shines most fully at the cross, the hour when the Son is glorified.

naos.gloss: Temple, sanctuary, the dwelling place of God. Jesus takes the word for the sacred building and applies it to His own body: destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up. The true meeting place between God and humanity is no longer a structure of stone but the crucified and risen Christ, in whom God dwells.

basic.context: John places two scenes side by side to show the new thing Jesus brings. At a village wedding the wine runs out, a social disaster, and Jesus quietly turns roughly a hundred and twenty gallons of washing water into the finest wine. John calls it the first of His signs and says it revealed His glory. Then, in Jerusalem at Passover, Jesus drives the traders from the temple and, challenged for a sign, speaks a riddle: destroy this temple and in three days I will raise it up. He meant His body.
basic.hermeneutics: The key is the word sign. These are not just miracles to amaze; they are pictures pointing to who Jesus is. The water for ritual washing becoming abundant wine hints that Jesus brings the joy and fullness the old rituals only anticipated. The temple scene raises the question, where do we now meet God? John answers, in the crucified and risen body of Jesus. Notice too that the disciples only understood the temple saying after the resurrection.
basic.originalLanguages: Two words carry the section. Jesus says His hora, His hour, has not yet come, the appointed time of His death and glory that the whole Gospel moves toward. And John names the miracle the first of His semeion, His signs, by which He revealed His doxa, His glory. In Jerusalem He redefines the naos, the temple, as His own body.
basic.typology: The old jars of purification water, replaced by wine, picture the old covenant order giving way to the joy of the messianic feast the prophets foretold. The temple of stone gives way to the true temple, the body of Christ, where God and humanity finally meet, destroyed at the cross and raised on the third day.
basic.christ: Both signs are about Christ. He is the true bridegroom who provides the best wine, the host of the feast of the age to come. He is the true temple, the place of God's presence, torn down in death and raised in three days. He knows every heart and needs no one to tell Him what is in a person.
basic.god: God is a God of abundant joy, not stingy religion; the wine is lavish and the best is saved for last. He is also jealous for true worship, so that His house is not made a marketplace. And He is present, no longer chiefly in a building but in His Son.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 25 and Amos 9 promise a feast of rich wine in the age to come. Psalm 69 supplies zeal for Your house. Revelation 21 shows the new creation where God dwells with His people and there is no temple but God and the Lamb.
basic.oneStory: The story is turning from shadow to substance. The washing rites and the temple pointed forward, and now the reality has come. Jesus brings the abundant wine of the promised feast and becomes Himself the true temple, the meeting place of God and humanity, opened to all through His death and resurrection.

context.literary:
The two scenes are joined by hinges the English hides. Verse 12 carries Jesus from Cana down to Capernaum, and verse 13 takes Him up to Jerusalem, so the chapter swings from a village to the capital, from a private family feast to the national festival, from joy to confrontation. Yet each scene repeats the same shape. A need or a corruption is exposed, Jesus acts, a puzzle is left in the air, and only later do people understand: the servants know where the wine came from, the master of the banquet does not, and the disciples grasp the temple saying only after the resurrection, verse 22.

The chapter is framed by signs. Verse 11 calls Cana 'the first of His signs,' and verse 23 says many saw 'the signs He was doing and believed in His name.' Then the closing two verses set a sombre note against that belief, with the verb for believe doing double duty: they 'believed in His name,' but Jesus 'did not entrust Himself to them.' In the Greek it is the same verb, so John is sounding a quiet alarm about faith that rests only on wonders.

Notice the careful movement in the temple scene between two Greek words that English renders alike. In verses 14 and 15 the 'temple courts' are the sacred precinct, the hieron, with its courtyards and trading. In the saying of verses 19 to 21 the word is naos, the sanctuary proper, the inner house where God dwelt. Jesus drives the traders from the precinct but claims the sanctuary for His own body. The scene also follows the old pattern of a prophetic act followed by a spoken sign, since the people demand a sign and receive a riddle.

Finally, the chapter works as a double opening. The wedding shows what Jesus gives, and the temple shows what He replaces. Both are placed before any teaching, as though the Gospel wants to say first that the old things are about to be fulfilled, and only then begin to explain how.
context.historical:
A village wedding in Galilee was a public event of days rather than hours, and the hosts carried the honour of the whole village. To run out of wine was a social disaster, a failure of hospitality that could shame a family for years. That is the pressure behind Mary's quiet remark in verse 3 and the reason the master of the banquet's reaction in verse 10 is a compliment of the highest order.

The six jars were stone, and the text says they were there 'for the Jewish rites of purification.' Stone was commonly held to resist ritual impurity in a way clay did not, which makes sense of why a pious household would keep large stone vessels for washing hands and utensils. Each held twenty to thirty gallons by the BSB's count, so Jesus supplies well over a hundred gallons. The sheer size matters in a village feast, and so does the fact that the vessels belonged to the system of ritual cleanness.

The Passover brought pilgrims to Jerusalem from across the Roman world, and the temple was crowded with commerce. Animals were needed for sacrifice, and the poor could offer doves, Leviticus 5:7. Foreign coins could not be used for the temple tax, which is why money changers sat at tables, Exodus 30:13. These were legitimate services, which makes the anger of Jesus sharper. The trade had grown up inside the precinct, so that the court where people from the nations might pray, Isaiah 56:7, was loud with commerce.

The 'forty-six years' of verse 20 matches what is known of Herod the Great's rebuilding of the temple, which began about 20 BC, and so places this scene in the late 20s AD. The work was not finished until decades after Jesus' day. The leaders' reply therefore comes from long, expensive experience: nobody rebuilds that in three days. The charge of speaking against the temple later surfaces at His trial, Mark 14:58, and at Stephen's, Acts 6:14, which shows how memorable and how easily twisted the saying was.
context.canonical:
The wine of Cana belongs with the Old Testament's picture of the age to come as a banquet. Isaiah 25:6 promises a feast of rich food and well aged wine on the mountain of the LORD, Amos 9:13 speaks of mountains dripping with sweet wine, and Joel 3:18 does the same. Jacob's blessing of Judah in Genesis 49:11-12 already pictures wine as the sign of a coming ruler. The prophets also speak of God as the husband of His people, Isaiah 62:5 and Hosea 2:19-20, which is why Jesus is later called the bridegroom by John the Baptist, John 3:29. Jesus Himself tells parables of wedding feasts, Matthew 22:1-14, and Revelation closes with the marriage supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:7-9.

The temple scene draws on a rich tradition of prophetic protest. Jeremiah 7:11 condemned making the house a den of robbers, and Isaiah 56:7 called it a house of prayer for all peoples. Malachi 3:1 promised that the Lord would come suddenly to His temple, and Zechariah 14:21 ended with the final purity of the house. The disciples recall Psalm 69:9, 'Zeal for Your house will consume Me,' a psalm of a righteous sufferer that the New Testament uses again of Christ, for instance in Romans 15:3.

The idea of the temple as the place where God dwells runs from the tabernacle, Exodus 25:8, through Solomon's temple, 1 Kings 8:10-11, to the vision of the future house in Ezekiel 40 to 48, whose river flows out to give life, Ezekiel 47:1. The New Testament then moves the language of temple onto Christ and His people. Believers together are God's temple, 1 Corinthians 3:16 and Ephesians 2:19-22, each believer's body is a temple of the Holy Spirit, 1 Corinthians 6:19, and the church is a spiritual house built of living stones, 1 Peter 2:5. Hebrews presents Christ as a high priest in the greater tabernacle, Hebrews 9:11, and Revelation sees no temple in the holy city, because its temple is the Lord God and the Lamb, Revelation 21:22.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John does not tell us that Jesus' mother was wrong to ask, nor that the traders were fraudulent, nor even how the water changed. He is working at a different level: he wants his readers to see the Word made flesh beginning to show what He came for. By calling the wine a sign and saying it revealed His glory, he tells readers to look through the miracle at its meaning, as he does throughout the Gospel and states outright in John 20:30-31.

The first readers were probably a mix of Jews and Greek speakers, some of whom had known the temple, and some of whom had seen it destroyed in AD 70 if the Gospel was written after that. For them the temple saying would be a source of comfort and challenge together. John wants them to learn that the loss of a building was not the loss of God's presence, since the sanctuary was never finally a place but a person.

He also writes to warn about shallow faith. The closing verses of the chapter place popular enthusiasm beside Jesus' reserve. It is possible to be impressed by signs and still not be someone to whom He can entrust Himself. This is not a harsh word but a call to the deeper kind of trust that the next chapter begins to describe through Nicodemus, a man who saw signs and came by night.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes events that happened once: a miracle at a particular wedding, a particular cleansing at a particular Passover, and a saying that was misunderstood until the resurrection. It does not prescribe that believers should expect water to become wine, nor does it turn the temple action into a blueprint for forceful protest in church life. Jesus acts with a unique authority as the Son, and the text itself explains that His zeal was for His Father's house.

Several points do carry forward. Mary's advice, 'Do whatever He tells you,' verse 5, is a general instruction that applies beyond that evening, and the servants who obey with no understanding at all become the first to know what happened. The chapter also confirms that Jesus cares about ordinary human joy, so that the gospel is not opposed to feasts and festivity. And the warning against turning a place of worship into a marketplace speaks to any age, though the application is to our own hearts first. Paul says believers are now God's temple, so the question of what we allow in the house points inward as much as outward.

debates.question: Why does Jesus call His mother 'Woman' and say His hour has not come, and then act?

views.label: A gentle rebuke that redefines the relationship
views.case: Jesus sets a distance between filial duty and His mission: He acts by the Father's timing, not at a family's request. 'Woman' and the idiom 'what is that to you and to Me' mark that boundary, and Mary's reply to the servants shows she understood.

views.label: A respectful address and a statement about timing
views.case: 'Woman' was a courteous form of address, and He uses it again from the cross, John 19:26, with tender care. The idiom signals that His agenda is not hers, not that He is cold. The hour in question is His death and glory, which He will not hasten by a request but will anticipate in a sign.

debates.bearing: Either way, Mary does not argue but entrusts the matter to Him and tells the servants to obey. Jesus then acts, which shows that His sign is given out of grace and not on demand, as a foretaste of the hour that He will not bring forward.

debates.question: Is the temple cleansing of John 2 the same event as in Matthew, Mark and Luke, or a second one?

views.label: Two separate cleansings
views.case: John places it at the start of the ministry and the Synoptics in the last week. The details differ: John mentions a whip and cattle and gives a different saying, and the leaders' demand for a sign is specific to John. Jesus could well have acted twice, since commerce in the courts would not have vanished after the first protest.

views.label: One event, placed thematically by John
views.case: Ancient writers often arranged material by theme rather than strict chronology. John puts the scene first to announce the replacement of the temple, and the Synoptics place it where it leads to the arrest. The overlap in the Isaiah and Jeremiah allusions and in the reaction of the authorities supports a single event.

debates.bearing: The Gospel's argument does not depend on the answer. In either case John's purpose is clear: the cleansing is the opening of the case about Jesus and the temple, and the saying about destroying it is the center.

debates.question: What does Jesus mean by 'this temple'?

views.label: His own body, spoken with a gesture
views.case: John says so in verse 21, and the word is naos, the sanctuary, not the precincts. The saying about three days points to the resurrection, which the disciples recalled afterward, verse 22.

views.label: The physical temple, with the body as secondary
views.case: Some hold that Jesus also speaks of the physical sanctuary's fate, whose destruction He foresaw, and that the verse joins the two. The accusations at His trial are taken as evidence that the saying was heard as about the building, Mark 14:58.

debates.bearing: The narrator's explanation is the controlling one, but the fact that listeners heard the building shows how well the saying served as a riddle. The old sanctuary was bound to pass, and the true one was already standing there.

study.originalLanguages:
Begin with Jesus' reply to His mother, 'Woman, what is that to you and to Me?' The Greek phrase is literally 'what to me and to you,' a Semitic idiom that appears in the Old Testament, for example in Judges 11:12 and 1 Kings 17:18, and in the Gospels in Mark 1:24. It does not have one fixed tone; it marks a difference of standpoint or agenda between speakers. In this context it keeps the question of who sets the timetable. The address 'Woman,' gynai, is not harsh, and Jesus will use it again at the cross, John 19:26, where He entrusts His mother to the beloved disciple. John never calls her by name, which is itself a quiet way of keeping her in a representative role.

The word 'hour,' hora, becomes one of the Gospel's key terms. Here it is 'not yet,' and the same note sounds in John 7:30 and 8:20, until Jesus says that it has come in John 12:23 and again in 13:1 and 17:1. Notice, then, that a wedding scene already refers to the cross: the wine runs out at the hour that is not yet, and the best wine is given at the hour that will come.

The word 'sign,' semeion, is the third key term. John does not usually call Jesus' works 'miracles' or 'mighty deeds' but signs, things that point beyond themselves. The numbering matters: this is the first, and 4:54 will call the healing of the official's son the second, bracketing the Galilean section. John 20:30-31 explains the choice, 'these are written that you may believe.' 'Glory,' doxa, in verse 11 is the same word as in John 1:14, so Cana is where the glory seen in the flesh begins to be displayed.

The temple vocabulary needs care. In verses 14 and 15 the word is hieron, the whole sacred precinct, and in verses 19 to 21 it is naos, the sanctuary where God was said to dwell. Jesus' claim about the naos is therefore sharper than a protest about the courts. The verb for 'raise' in verses 19 and 22, egeiro, is the ordinary word for rising from sleep or from death. In the saying Jesus says 'I will raise it,' which gives Him an active part in His own resurrection, while elsewhere in the New Testament the Father is said to raise Him, as in Acts 2:24, and the Gospel holds both truths together.

Finally, look at the verb 'believed' in verses 23 and 24. People 'believed in His name' because of the signs, but Jesus 'did not entrust Himself to them.' The Greek verb is the same, pisteuo. John is saying that a faith which depends on wonders is, as it were, not yet the kind of faith that He can trust. It is a rare thing for a Gospel to tell us that the Lord held back from believers, and that is why the next scene begins with a man who also believes in the signs, John 3:2.

typology.type: The six stone jars of ritual washing
typology.fulfillment: The jars belonged to the system by which Israel kept clean for worship. Jesus fills them with water and the servants draw out wine, and the contents are better than the water that came before. The correspondence is that what was set apart for purification is made a vessel of abundance. The escalation is from outward washing to the gladness of the age to come, which the prophets described as a feast, Isaiah 25:6. Paul and Hebrews speak of the old regulations as external, concerned with food and drink and various washings, until the time of reformation, Hebrews 9:10. The type falls short in that the jars did not make anyone clean within, and the text does not say the rites were wrong, only that they were waiting for something.

typology.type: The bridegroom and the wedding feast
typology.fulfillment: The prophets spoke of God rejoicing over His people as a bridegroom over his bride, Isaiah 62:5, and Jesus appears at a wedding as the one who supplies what the bridegroom lacked. The Baptist will say in John 3:29 that the bride belongs to the bridegroom, and Jesus calls Himself the bridegroom in Mark 2:19-20. The escalation is that God's own presence at the feast is not a figure of speech but a person. The type falls short in that the earthly bridegroom of Cana remains unnamed and unremarkable, while the true Bridegroom's wedding is still ahead, Revelation 19:7.

typology.type: The temple as the house where God dwells
typology.fulfillment: The tabernacle and temple were the place of God's name and presence, Exodus 25:8 and 1 Kings 8:10-11. Jesus takes the word naos and applies it to His body, so that the place where heaven and earth meet is now a person who will be struck down and raised. The New Testament extends it: in Him the fullness of deity dwells bodily, Colossians 2:9, and believers are built into a dwelling for God, Ephesians 2:21-22. The type falls short in that the building could be destroyed without ending anything, whereas this temple's destruction is the means by which it is raised, never to be pulled down again.

The phrase 'in three days' at the end of the chapter and 'on the third day' at its start frame the whole unit. The third day is a note of deliverance and vindication in the Old Testament, for instance in Genesis 22:4 and Hosea 6:2, and the New Testament declares that Christ was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, 1 Corinthians 15:4. Cana's third day is not itself a prophecy, but the author may well have wished readers to hear the word. We should hold the link lightly, since it is a resonance and not a proof, and the clear typological claim rests on verse 21.

study.christ:
This chapter shows Christ as the one who brings what the old order promised, and it does so in two movements that turn on each other.

At Cana He is the host and giver of joy. The wine that fails is the sign of an order that cannot supply what it announces, and the Gospel makes the gift lavish: many jars, to the brim, and the best saved until last. The prophets said the age to come would be a feast, Isaiah 25:6, and John says that its first taste has been given in an obscure village. The remark about the best wine kept until now, verse 10, becomes a miniature of the whole Gospel. The old covenant was good, but God has kept the best for the end, as Hebrews says that God has spoken in these last days by His Son, Hebrews 1:1-2.

Notice also how He acts. Jesus does not pronounce a word and display power; He tells servants to fill the jars, and then to draw. The sign is hidden in obedience, and only the servants know. This is the pattern of His glory in John: it is revealed to those who do what He says. It is also tied to His hour. The sign at Cana gestures towards a death and glory that the Gospel counts as His real revelation, John 12:23-24, and the wine that gladdens and the blood of the cross meet in the supper, John 6:53-56 and Luke 22:20.

In Jerusalem He is the true temple and its zealous Lord. His zeal for the Father's house, verse 17, fulfils the psalmist's cry and shows His complete loyalty to the Father, which is also the loyalty of the Son in the garden. He demands that the place of meeting with God be a place of prayer for all nations. Then He turns the question of His authority into a claim that the whole system of sanctuary now rests on Him: if this temple is destroyed, He will raise it. The believing reader hears the resurrection and sees that the place of God's presence is the crucified and risen Jesus, so that every later claim about access to God, from the torn veil in Matthew 27:51 to the new and living way of Hebrews 10:19-20, is anchored in this saying.

The final verses show another side of Christ. He 'knew what was in a man,' verse 25. This is the divine knowledge that the Old Testament reserves to God, who searches hearts, 1 Kings 8:39 and Jeremiah 17:10. It prepares for the picture of Nathanael and the Samaritan woman, for the knowledge that sees through a crowd to a single person. It also means He cannot be fooled by applause: the Lord who welcomes sinners is not the Lord who can be managed by enthusiasm.

A caution is needed. The wine is not a code for the blood of the cross, and the six jars are not six ages. The links drawn in the New Testament itself are the temple saying, the hour, and the bridegroom. If a detail is not taken up by the text or by later Scripture, it is better left as a detail.
study.god:
The chapter shows a God of lavish gladness. The wine is not a bare necessity; it is abundance, the best, given where there was shame. This corrects a certain picture of God as a severe taskmaster. The God of the Bible made the feast, and He is pleased to share the joy of a family, so worship in this Gospel is not hostile to gladness. Psalm 104:15 lists wine among the good gifts that gladden the heart, and John sees them fulfilled in Jesus.

God is also jealous for the honour of His name and the purity of worship. The cleansing of the temple, with its allusion to the psalm of zeal, shows that the same God who gives freely will not tolerate a corrupt approach to Himself. Holiness and generosity are not rivals here. The wine and the whip come from one character, and both express what the Father is like in the Son. In the Old Testament the same holiness is at work in the cloud filling the house, 1 Kings 8:10-11, and the same God warns against treating His house as a refuge for wrongdoing, Jeremiah 7:9-11.

The chapter also teaches that God keeps His own timetable. The 'hour' language shows that the Father has appointed times, so that even a compassionate request cannot hasten the work that He has set. Divine sovereignty and divine compassion go together: Jesus is in no hurry, but He is not indifferent. He acts at Cana within the rhythm of an appointed plan, and the first sign points forward to the time that He alone can bring.

God is shown as present among His people in a new way. For centuries the place of God's name was a sanctuary; now His presence has come in the Son. The doctrine of the incarnation is here applied to worship: where do we meet God, and in whom? The answer shapes how Christians pray, in Jesus' name, and how they gather, as a house built of living stones.

Finally, God is the one who knows. 'He knew what was in a man' means that nothing is hidden, and for worship this is both comfort and warning. We can come honestly, since He is not misled by performance. And we cannot trade on our outward religion, since He looks at the heart. The same Lord who did not entrust Himself to the crowd invites us to a trust that is real, and He is the one who makes it possible by giving the Spirit, as the next chapter shows.

crossReferences.note: A feast of rich food and well aged wine for all peoples on the LORD's mountain. This is the promise behind the joy of Cana, and it links the abundance of the wine with the age to come, so that the first sign is a taste of what the prophets said God would one day spread for the nations.

The prophet describes a day when the mountains drip with sweet wine, after the restoration of David's fallen house. Like Isaiah 25, it ties abundant wine to messianic renewal, and so supports reading the sheer volume of wine at Cana as meaningful and not merely marvelous.

As a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so will your God rejoice over you. The wedding setting of the first sign draws on this picture of God as husband to His people, and it prepares for the Baptist's words about the bridegroom's voice in John 3:29.

The verse the disciples remember in verse 17. The psalm is the prayer of a righteous sufferer consumed by zeal for God's house and reproached for it, so the disciples' memory already carries a shadow of the cost that this zeal will have for Jesus.

God's house will be called a house of prayer for all peoples. The trading was set up in the precinct that was meant for the nations, and so Jesus' cleansing is concerned with access as well as purity: the place where outsiders could pray had been given over to commerce.

The Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to His temple. The sudden entry of Jesus into the courts, after the Baptist's role as messenger in the previous chapter, fits this promise, and it explains why the confrontation is about authority and not simply about manners.

At His trial, witnesses misquote the temple saying, claiming He said He would destroy the temple made with hands and build another not made with hands. This shows how widely the saying circulated and how it could be twisted, and it supports the Gospel's note that its meaning was only seen after Easter.

Paul tells the church that they are God's temple and that God's Spirit dwells in them. The shift from stone to people, grounded in the body of Christ, is the apostolic outworking of John 2:21, and it makes the saying about the temple a statement about the church as well.

Believers are joined together as a holy temple in the Lord, with Christ Jesus as the cornerstone. Paul uses the building imagery that John 2 applies to Christ's body, extending it to include Gentiles who were once far off, so the cleansed temple becomes an open one.

Nicodemus comes because of the signs, which links directly to the final verses of chapter 2. He is a man who believes at some level because of what he has seen, and the conversation shows what it means to be taken from sign-based interest to the new birth.

John sees no temple in the new Jerusalem, because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple. The saying of John 2:19 reaches its end here, where the presence that the sanctuary only pointed to fills everything and nothing separates people from God.

study.oneStory:
From the beginning God made a place to dwell with His people. Eden was a sanctuary where God walked, and the expulsion of Genesis 3 was the loss of it. Tabernacle and temple were the long answer: a small piece of ground where heaven touched earth, guarded by cherubim and hedged with rules about washing and offering. Alongside that sanctuary ran a second line of hope, that the broken joy of the world would be restored in a feast. The prophets spoke of a banquet for the nations and a bridegroom who would rejoice over his people, and they promised that the glory would come back to the house.

This chapter is the moment those two lines meet in one man. At a wedding He provides the joy that the old order could only announce, and in the temple He claims to be the place where God and people meet. It answers what the story left unresolved: how can a sinful people live in the presence of a holy God, and how can the sorrow of a cursed world be turned to gladness? Not by more rules and more washing but by a person in whom both are accomplished.

It also sets up what follows. The sign of destroying and raising points to the cross and the empty tomb, and the hour that has not yet come is the hour of John 12 and 13. The theme of the temple continues with the woman at the well, who is told that worship will no longer be tied to one mountain or to Jerusalem, John 4:21-24, and in the Gospel's later chapters it reaches the promise of the Spirit flowing like living water, John 7:37-39. Acts shows the early church worshipping at the temple and then without it, and the epistles speak of believers as a temple of the Spirit.

The story ends in a city without a temple building, because God Himself is there, Revelation 21:22, and with a wedding supper, Revelation 19:9, where the best wine has been kept until now. The Cana feast is the first small sign of that last feast, and the cleansed courts are the first small sign of a world where no one will sell or exclude, and where, as the last chapters say, the nations will walk by His light, Revelation 21:24.

quiz.q: Why does John call the turning of water into wine the first of Jesus' signs?

options.text: Because it points beyond itself to who Jesus is and reveals His glory, leading the disciples to believe.
options.note: Verse 11 states the sign revealed His glory and led to faith; signs are meant to be read.

options.text: Because it was the most impressive miracle He ever did.
options.note: John's point is not scale but meaning; a sign points to Jesus' identity, not merely amazes.

options.text: Because it showed His power and provided joy at the feast.
options.note: True as far as it goes, but the deeper point is that the sign reveals His glory and calls forth belief.

options.text: Because it proved He approved of every celebration.
options.note: The sign is about revealing Jesus' glory, not a general endorsement of parties.

quiz.q: What does Jesus mean by destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up?

options.text: He is speaking of the temple of His body, His death and resurrection on the third day.
options.note: Verse 21 explains He spoke of His body; the true temple is the risen Christ.

options.text: He is promising to rebuild Herod's temple supernaturally.
options.note: Verse 21 rules this out; He was not speaking of the stone building.

options.text: He is pointing to the resurrection as the sign of His authority.
options.note: True that His resurrection is the sign, but the answer omits that the temple He means is His own body.

options.text: He is predicting the temple's future destruction by Rome.
options.note: That destruction did come later, but here Jesus speaks of His body, not the Roman siege.

quiz.q: What is the significance of the water jars being for the Jewish rites of purification?

options.text: Jesus transforms the water of the old ritual order into the abundant wine of the messianic feast.
options.note: The detail signals the old order giving way to the joy and fullness Jesus brings.

options.text: It shows Jesus disregarded Jewish law entirely.
options.note: Jesus fulfills rather than despises the law; He brings what the rites anticipated.

options.text: It shows Jesus provided a large quantity of wine.
options.note: The quantity is real, but the point is the purification jars becoming the vessels of new joy.

options.text: It hints that Jesus brings something greater than the old washings.
options.note: Right direction, but it stops short of the specific picture of the messianic feast of wine.

quiz.q: Why did Jesus not entrust Himself to those who believed because of His signs, verses 23 to 25?

options.text: Because He knew every heart and knew their belief was shallow.
options.note: Verses 24 and 25 say He knew what was in each person; He was not deceived by sign-based enthusiasm.

options.text: Because He disliked crowds.
options.note: The reason given is His knowledge of hearts, not any dislike of people.

options.text: Because belief based only on signs can be unreliable.
options.note: True and implied, but the text grounds it specifically in Jesus' knowledge of what was in each person.

options.text: Because He wanted to keep His identity secret a while longer.
options.note: There is a theme of the hour, but the stated reason is His knowledge of their hearts, not secrecy.

quiz.q: What does Jesus reveal about God in cleansing the temple?

options.text: That God is jealous for true worship and will not have His house made a marketplace.
options.note: Verse 16 and the zeal of Psalm 69 show God's holy concern for pure worship.

options.text: That God is indifferent to how He is worshiped.
options.note: The opposite; Jesus' zeal shows God cares intensely about the purity of worship.

options.text: That God opposes all buying and selling anywhere.
options.note: The issue is corrupting His house, not commerce in general.

options.text: That God's house is meant for prayer and His presence, not profit.
options.note: True and close, but it softens the sharp note of God's jealous zeal for His house.

questions: At Cana Jesus saved the best wine for last. Where are you tempted to think the joy God gives is thin or second-rate, when He means to give His finest?
Mary told the servants, do whatever He tells you. What is Jesus telling you to do that you have been hesitant to obey?
Jesus was consumed with zeal for His Father's house. What has crept into your worship of God that needs to be driven out?
The disciples only understood the temple saying after the resurrection. Where might you need to trust Jesus' words now and wait for understanding to come later?
Jesus knew what was in every heart and was not fooled by shallow enthusiasm. How does it change your walk with Him to know that He sees you completely and still calls you His own?

translationNotes.note: Twenty to thirty gallons renders the Greek measure; the BSB footnote gives two or three metretae, about 20.8 to 31.2 gallons or 78.8 to 118.1 liters each, so the six jars held a lavish quantity.
Temple courts renders a word the BSB footnote notes is literally the temple, also in verse 15; the trade filled the outer courts, the court of the Gentiles.
Zeal for Your house will consume Me quotes Psalm 69:9, a psalm of the righteous sufferer that the disciples saw fulfilled in Jesus.
